commonErrors.example: A learner writes on the worksheet that every mutation harms the organism.

fixIt.corrected: Most mutations are neutral: only some are harmful, and a rare few are the raw material of evolution.
fixIt.prompt: Fix it: state what most mutations do, and why a changed base can leave the protein job unchanged.

commonErrors.example: On the exit ticket, a learner picks the statement that every mutation harms the organism.

fixIt.corrected: Most mutations are neutral because the protein still does its job, so harm is the exception, not the rule.
fixIt.prompt: Fix it: explain in one sentence why the mutated gene in scene s5 still builds a working protein.

modelAnswers.answer: DNA is transcribed into mRNA in the nucleus, and the mRNA is translated into a polypeptide at a ribosome in the cytoplasm.
modelAnswers.question: Outline the central dogma in one or two sentences, naming where transcription and translation happen.

modelAnswers.answer: A son has only one X chromosome, so the recessive h allele has no second allele to mask it and the trait shows; a daughter has a second X carrying H, which masks h, so she is a carrier without symptoms.
modelAnswers.question: A carrier mother (X^H X^h) and a normal father (X^H Y) have children. Explain why a son who inherits X^h has haemophilia, while a daughter who inherits X^h usually does not.

nextSteps: Reteach the mutation trap from the paired notes trap before any further genetics work: most sequence changes are neutral because the protein still does its job.
Practise sex-linked crosses from scene s4, checking each son against the single X he inherits from his mother.
strengths: Most of the class can outline the central dogma in the right order, naming transcription in the nucleus and translation at a ribosome.
The class can work the monohybrid square to the 3:1 phenotype ratio and the 1:2:1 genotype ratio.
